name: PRP under eyes

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is made by drawing a person's blood and spinning it to concentrate platelets. Clinics offer it under the eyes for thin, crepey or dark skin, promoted for wrinkles and fine lines, aiming for thicker, smoother-looking under-eye skin.

Platelets carry growth factors and cytokines, and proponents propose these support tissue repair and skin quality. Wikipedia describes PRP evidence as mixed and condition-specific. No published trial of PRP specifically for under-eye skin was found, and a registered trial in the nasojugal fold (tear trough) was withdrawn.

paras: Clinics inject it under the eyes or apply it after microneedling, usually as a series of sessions. Preparation methods vary by kit and facility, and results are judged over weeks as skin quality changes.

Adverse effects are generally low in trials. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, and clinic use is considered off-label. In 2024 the CDC reported HIV cases linked to an unlicensed spa that reused contaminated equipment.

angle.text: Users get PRP injections under the eyes to improve thin, crepey or dark skin, drawing on clinic marketing for wrinkles and fine lines. Growth factors from your own platelets are thought to support skin repair and thickness. Eye-specific trial data is limited.

lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is a concentrate of plasma from a person's own blood, produced by centrifugation, that retains platelets and the growth factors they carry.[1] Clinics promote PRP injections for wrinkles, fine lines and similar skin concerns, and the under-eye area is one site discussed for thin skin.[1]

Wikipedia describes the evidence for PRP as mixed and condition-specific, with stronger support for some wound types and weak or negative findings for several musculoskeletal uses.[1] No published trial of PRP specifically for under-eye skin was found; a registered trial in the nasojugal folds was withdrawn.[2]
infobox: Intradermal or subdermal injection, sometimes with microneedling
Preparation devices cleared; clinical use off-label

paras: Blood is spun in a centrifuge to remove red cells while keeping platelets, which carry growth factors that may support tissue healing.[1] Preparation varies between facilities and kits, so results can differ.[1]
Clinics promote PRP for wrinkles, fine lines, blemishes and hair loss.[1] So-called vampire facials, which often combine PRP with microneedling, grew popular in the 2010s.[1]

Adverse effects are generally low across trials, and one review found weak evidence of harm at similar rates in treated and untreated people.[1] In 2024 the CDC reported HIV cases among clients of an unlicensed New Mexico spa that reused contaminated equipment.[1]

No studies found for under-eye PRP among the sources reviewed. A registered trial of PRP administration in the nasojugal folds (NCT03255681) was withdrawn.[2] A completed phase 2/3 study (NCT01461785, n=25) evaluated PRP in fat transfer, a related but different use.[3]

timeline.event: The term platelet-rich plasma is first used.[1]
First reported use in Italy during open heart surgery.[1]
